intro:
## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Numbers

1. Preparing to leave Sinai (1:1–10:10)
  A. Counting and assembling the tribes (1:1–4:49)
  B. Regulations (5:1–6:27)
  C. Dedicating the altar (7:1–89)
  D. Setting up the lampstand (8:1–4)
  E. Setting apart the Levites (8:5–29)
  F. Second Passover; the cloud to lead them; trumpets (9:1–10:10)
2. Sinai to Moab, through the wilderness (10:11–17:13)
  A. Complaining and murmuring (10:11–11:15)
  B. The quails (11:16–35)
  C. Miriam’s leprosy (12:1–16)
  D. The spies selected and sent (13:1–14:45)
  E. Commands (15:1–41)
  F. Korah’s rebellion (16:1–17:13)
3. The Priests and purifying (18:1–19:22)
  A. Priests and Levites (18:1–32)
  B. The law about purifying (19:1–22)
4. Conflicts (20:1–21:35)
  A. Miriam’s death (20:1–13)
  B. Edom’s refusal and Aaron’s death (20:14–29)
  C. Journey to Moab (21:1–35)
5. The Plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
  A. Balaam (22:1–24:25)
  B. Baal Peor (25:1–18)
  C. The second counting (26:1–65)
  D. Inheritance rights for daughters (27:1–11)
  E. Joshua succeeds Moses (27:12–23)
  F. Offerings and women’s vows (28:1–30:16)
  G. Midianite war (31:1–54)
  H. Across the Jordan (32:1–42)
  I. The people set up camp (33:1–56)
  J. Land west of the Jordan; cities for Levites and cities of refuge (34:1–35:34)
  K. Female heirs marry (36:1–13)

### What is the book of Numbers about?

The book of Numbers tells about the people of Israel as they traveled from Mount Sinai in the wilderness to the Jordan River. While traveling, the Israelites became discouraged. So they rebelled against the leaders whom God had given them. At the Jordan River, the people of Israel refused to enter the Promised Land. Because the Israelites were afraid and did not trust God, he delayed their entry into the Promised Land for 40 years (13:1–14:45).

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The title of this book, “Numbers,” refers to when the number of the Israelites was counted. The people of the project language may already be familiar with the name “Numbers” from other Bible versions. If not, the translator could consider a clearer name for the book, such as “The Counting of the People of Israel.”

### Who wrote the book of Numbers?

The writers of both the Old and New Testaments present Moses as being very involved with writing the book of Numbers. Since ancient times, both Jews and Christians have thought that Moses wrote Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### How does Numbers present the idea of the whole community being responsible when only a few people sinned?

The people understood and assumed that God would punish the whole community of Israel if some of the people rebelled against him. God did often punish the entire nation when some of them sinned. All of the people in the ancient Near East would have understood and expected this. However, Moses and Aaron prayed for God to punish only those who were guilty.

chapters.1:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is intended to form a smooth transition from the last chapter of the book of Leviticus. It describes the counting of Israelite men who are able to fight in the army.

1. Yahweh commands Moses to take a census of Israel’s fighting men (1–46)
2. Yahweh sets apart the Levites for service of the tabernacle (47–53)
3. Israel obeys Yahweh’s commands concerning the census (54)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Census

In this chapter, Yahweh commands Moses and Aaron to count how many men of military age were in each tribe of Israel. Some of these men were also called to lead their family groups.
chapters.2:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes how the tribes are to camp around the tabernacle. It also establishes the order in which they are to travel.

1. Yahweh assigns the tribes their camp positions and order of travel (1–31)
2. Israel camps and travels according to Yahweh’s commands (32–34)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cardinal directions

Yahweh explains how the Israelites will camp in relation to the sacred tent and does so using cardinal directions: north, east, south, and west. These terms describe a person’s orientation in relation to the sunrise. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If one faces the direction of the sunrise and then turns to his right, he is facing south. If, when facing the sunrise, he turns left, he is facing north.

### Banners

Each of the four camps (each made up of three tribes) would have its own “banner.” A banner is a type of flag that has images and sometimes words on it. In this case, the specific images and possibly words would indicate which tribes would camp near that banner. The banner was most closely connected with the tribe that was the leader of the camp: Judah, Reuben, Ephraim, and Dan.

### The order of the tribes

Here is a diagram of the tribes around the tent of meeting. Note the groups of three on each of the four cardinal directions.

```
          Asher         Dan           Naphtali

Benjamin              Levites                     Issachar

Ephraim            Tent of Meeting                   Judah

Manasseh                                           Zebulun

          Gad           Reuben        Simeon
```
chapters.3:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes the counting of Levite men and their assignments for taking care of the tent of meeting. It also describes how the Levites and their animals act as ransoms for the firstborn Israelites and the Israelites’ firstborn animals.

1. Aaron’s sons serve as priests (1–4)
2. Yahweh sets apart the Levites to serve the priests and care for the tabernacle (5–13)
3. Yahweh commands Moses to count the Levite clans and assigns their duties (14–39)
4. The Levites replace Israel’s firstborn, and the remaining firstborn are redeemed (40–51)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The tribe of Levi

The Levites had a special role in Israel, which is why they were not included in the census in chapters 1 and 2. They were specially dedicated to serve Yahweh and to keep and serve the sacred tent. They also functioned as a ransom for the firstborn Israelites and the firstborn animals of the Israelites. See the following entries for more information on the specific roles the Levites fulfilled.

### Keep

One of the primary duties of the Levites was to “keep” various things, including Aaron, the Israelites, and the parts of the sacred tent. In this context, “keep” refers specifically to keeping watch or guarding. No one besides the Levites was supposed to approach the sacred tent or do any priestly duties. So, the Levites guarded the sacred tent and the Israelites to prevent any non-Levite from approaching. Consider how to refer to this type of guard duty.

### Serve

One of the primary duties of the Levites was to “serve.” In this context, “serve” refers specifically to physical labor, including carrying, setting up, and tearing down the sacred tent and its equipment. There is more information about the physical labor required of the Levites in Numbers 4. Consider how to refer to this type of physical labor.

### Ransom

In 3:45–51, Yahweh requires the Israelites to pay a ransom to him for the firstborn males that he did not kill during the tenth plague in Egypt, as described in Exodus 12:29 and 13:15. Because Yahweh did not kill the firstborn male people and animals among the Israelites, he considered them to owe him their lives. Instead of taking their lives, Yahweh chose the Levite men to be his special servants in their place. However, the number of Levites was 273 people less than the number of firstborn males, so Yahweh required the people to pay money to him to redeem those additional people.

### “House of the father” and “clan”

The phrase “house of the father” and the word “clan” refer to divisions of an Israelite tribe. In Numbers, the “house of the father” was the larger division, and each “house of the father” contained several “clans.” For example, one “house of the father” within the tribe of Levi was named after Levi’s son, Gershon. Within the “house of the father” of the Gershonites were two clans named after Gershon’s sons (Levi’s grandsons): Libni and Shimei. Consider how you might refer to tribal divisions within other tribal divisions.

### Firstborn

Throughout this chapter, the word “firstborn” always refers to the oldest male child or offspring of a human or animal. Sometimes the word “male” is explicitly included, and other times it is implied. Use a word or phrase that clearly refers to the oldest male child or offspring.
chapters.4:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes the assignments Yahweh gave to each of the families who descended from Levi with regard to taking care of and transporting the sacred tent.

1. Yahweh assigns the Kohathites to carry the most holy things (1–20)
2. Yahweh assigns the Gershonites to carry the tabernacle’s curtains and coverings (21–28)
3. Yahweh assigns the Merarites to carry the tabernacle’s frames, posts, and bases (29–33)
4. Moses, Aaron, and Israel’s leaders count the Levites eligible for service (34–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### “Keeping,” “service,” and “burden”

As in the previous chapter, the word “keeping” refers to keeping watch or guarding. No one else was supposed to approach the sacred items, so the Levites were required to guard these items, especially when they were transporting them. The word “service” refers to physical labor, particularly taking down and setting up the sacred tent and the items that were in it. The Levites were also responsible for these tasks. Finally, the word “burden” refers to the specific task of carrying the pieces of the sacred tent and the items in it when the Israelites moved from one campsite to another. See how you translated “keeping” and “service” in chapter 3.

### “Clan” and “house of their fathers”

As in chapter 3, the phrase “house of the father” and the word “clan” refer to divisions of an Israelite tribe. The “house of the father” was the larger division, and each “house of the father” contained several “clans.” For example, one “house of the father” within the tribe of Levi was named after Levi’s son, Gershon. Within the “house of the father” of the Gershonites were two clans named after Gershon’s sons (Levi’s grandsons): Libni and Shimei. Translate “house of the father” and “clan” as you did in chapter 3.

### “Skin of a porpoise”

This phrase refers to leather made from the skin of a specific animal. Scholars debate exactly what animal the word refers to. Some argue that it is a land animal like a goat. Others argue that it is a sea animal like a dolphin or porpoise. The ULT identifies the animal as a porpoise, and the UST models how to refer to leather without identifying the animal. Consider how the word is translated in any translations your readers might know. If you do identify a specific animal, you could include a footnote indicating that this identification is uncertain.
chapters.5:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter gives instructions for keeping the camp pure because Yahweh lives among his people. It addresses ceremonial uncleanness, repayment for wrongdoing, and what to do when a husband suspects his wife has been unfaithful.

1. Yahweh commands Israel to send ceremonially unclean people outside the camp (1–4)
2. Yahweh gives instructions for confessing sins and making repayment (5–10)
3. Yahweh gives instructions on what to do when a husband suspects his wife has been unfaithful (11–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncleanness

When people or things are unclean, or impure, they are not fit to be in or near God’s presence. Uncleanness can be caused by sin, but it can also be caused by diseases or events that are not sinful. In 5:2–3, the uncleanness comes from diseases or from contact with a corpse. While having a disease or coming into contact with a corpse is not sinful, it still causes uncleanness. On the other hand, a wife who commits adultery, as discussed later in the chapter, is also unclean. This is because of the sin of adultery. With or without sin as the cause of the uncleanness, unclean people should not be in or near God’s presence.

### Guilt

In 5:6–8, the word “guilt” can refer both to the fact that someone did something wrong and to the restitution that the person must pay because he or she did something wrong. Because the person has “guilt” (he or she did something wrong), he or she must return the “guilt” (the payment for restitution) to the person he or she sinned against. See the notes on these verses for translation examples.

### Ceremony for a jealous husband

In 5:11–31, Yahweh tells Moses what a man should do when he thinks his wife has committed adultery. The instructions state that the man does not have direct proof, so they pertain only when he is suspicious. The ceremony includes an oath with a curse that the wife speaks, special water that she drinks, and a grain offering. Yahweh promises that he will punish any wife who has actually committed adultery, but he will not punish any wife who is innocent. The punishment is sickness or failure in reproductive organs so that the guilty wife will no longer be able to have children. It is important that Yahweh is the one who brings the punishment or not. The ceremony itself has no effect without Yahweh.
chapters.6:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter outlines laws for Nazirites (people who dedicate themselves to Yahweh in a special way and for a specific period of time). These laws indicate what the Nazirites must abstain from, what to do if they become unclean before the end of their time as Nazirites, and the sacrifices they should offer once they complete their time as Nazirites. The chapter ends with a blessing that the priests pronounce over the Israelites.

1. Yahweh gives instructions for the Nazirite vow (1–21)
2. Yahweh instructs Aaron and his sons to bless Israel (22–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Nazirite vow

The term “Nazirite” refers to someone who has vowed to separate himself or herself to Yahweh for a period of time. This period of time could be the person’s entire life, as in the case of Samson. Nazirites had to avoid three things: (1) eating or drinking anything produced from grapes or with any alcoholic content, (2) cutting their hair, (3) coming into contact with dead bodies. If any Nazirite came into contact with a dead body, he or she had to offer sacrifices and restart the time of separation. Once the time was complete, each Nazirite had to shave off his or her hair and offer a specific set of sacrifices. He or she could also offer more than what was required.

### Priestly blessing

In 6:24–26, Yahweh provides a blessing that the priests should speak to the Israelites. This blessing asks Yahweh to protect, care for, and give peace to the Israelites. Yahweh then promises that he will indeed carry out what this blessing asks. Consider how you might express a blessing in your language.
chapters.7:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter lists the offerings that each leader of the 12 Israelite tribes gave to Yahweh after Moses dedicated the altar.

1. The tribal leaders provide wagons and oxen for the Levites’ work (1–9)
2. Each tribal leader brings offerings for the dedication of the altar (10–88)
3. Moses hears Yahweh speaking from above the atonement lid (89)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Anointing and dedicating the altar

To set the altar apart for Yahweh, Moses poured olive oil on it. This was the “dedication” of the altar. After Moses did this, the leaders of the 12 tribes presented offerings to Yahweh, which Yahweh told Moses to give to the Levites. These offerings were called a “dedication,” since they were presented at the dedication of the altar.

### The offerings

The leaders of the 12 Israelite tribes together presented six wagons and 12 oxen. The Levites would use these wagons and oxen as they set up, took down, and transported the sacred tent. Then, on successive days, each of the 12 leaders presented an offering to Yahweh. Each offering was identical to the others and included a silver dish and basin with flour and oil filling them, a small bowl or ladle with incense filling it, and animals for a burnt offering (a bull, a ram, and a male lamb), for a sin offering (a male goat), and for a peace offering (two cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs). The priests would use the animals, flour, and incense to make sacrifices to Yahweh. The priests would use the dishes, basins, and ladles regularly during their work at the sacred tent.

### The shekel of the holy place

A “shekel” is a standard of weight. There were several different definitions of the weight of a “shekel.” The phrase “the shekel of the holy place” identifies a specific definition: the one used by the priests at the sacred tent. This shekel weighed about 11 grams. Throughout this chapter, the author makes it clear that it is this weight for “shekel” that the leaders used to weigh the gold and silver dishes that they presented to Yahweh.
chapters.8:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter details the cleansing and consecration of the Levites so that they could serve at the sacred tent. It also provides brief instructions on the orientation of the lamps on the lampstand and on the age requirements for service at the tent.

1. Yahweh gives instructions for arranging the seven lamps (1–4)
2. The Levites are purified and presented to Yahweh for service (5–22)
3. Yahweh establishes the ages for the Levites’ service (23–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cleansing and consecrating the Levites

In this chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to cleanse and consecrate the Levites. 8:6–7 gives instructions for cleansing them: they must be sprinkled with water, shave off their hair, and wash their clothing. 8:8–14 gives instructions for consecrating them after they have been cleansed: they must offer two bulls, and they must be presented like a raised offering to Yahweh. 8:15 gives a clear summary: in order to serve at the sacred tent, the Levites need to be cleansed and consecrated like a raised offering.

### “Service” and “keeping”

As in Numbers 3–4, the word “keeping” refers to keeping watch or guarding. No one else was supposed to approach the sacred items, so the Levites were required to guard these items, especially when they were transporting them. 8:26 includes an unusual plural form: “keepings.” It probably refers to all the kinds of guard duty the Levites might need to perform. The word “service” refers to physical labor, particularly taking down and setting up the sacred tent and the items that were in it. The Levites were also responsible for these tasks. See how you translated “keeping” and “service” in Numbers 3–4.

### The Levites and the firstborn Israelites

As outlined in chapter 3, Yahweh required the Israelites to pay a ransom to him for the firstborn males that he did not kill during the tenth plague in Egypt, as described in Exodus 12:29 and 13:15. Because Yahweh did not kill the firstborn male people and animals among the Israelites, he considered them to owe him their lives. Instead of taking their lives, Yahweh chose the Levite men to be his special servants in their place. Yahweh repeats some of that information in 8:17–18. See how you translated the similar statements in Numbers 3.
chapters.9:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter briefly narrates how the Israelites celebrated the Passover for the first time since they left Egypt, and it also gives instructions for a celebration of the Passover in the second month for those who were unable to celebrate it in the first month. Then, the author describes how a cloud visually represented Yahweh’s commands to the Israelites concerning when to travel and where to camp.

1. Israel celebrates the Passover, and Yahweh provides for those unable to celebrate at the appointed time (1–14)
2. Yahweh uses the cloud over the tabernacle to show Israel when to camp and when to travel (15–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Passover

The Passover was a festival that celebrated how God delivered the Israelites from Egypt. You can read more about the Passover in Exodus 12. This chapter records the first celebration of this festival after God delivered the Israelites from Egypt. The festival was celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month, and it included a special meal at which the Israelites ate unleavened bread and a special lamb. In this chapter, Yahweh allows any Israelites who were unable to celebrate on that day (because of impurity or travel) to celebrate on a backup day, which was the fourteenth day of the second month. This festival was a very important one, so Yahweh indicates that anyone who chooses not to celebrate it must be expelled from the community.

### Being “cut off” from the people

The punishment for failing to celebrate the Passover (except for impurity or travel) was being “cut off” from the rest of the Israelites. Scholars are unsure exactly what penalty this phrase implies. It could refer to death by execution. It could refer to punishment from Yahweh in a way of his choice. It could refer to expulsion from the Israelite community. The UST and notes follow this last option. If possible, use a word or phrase that could be understood in several of these ways. If you must specify, it is recommended that you follow the UST and notes.

### The cloud

This chapter refers to “the cloud” that was over the sacred tent during the Israelites’ travels in the wilderness. This cloud appeared when the Israelites left Egypt (see Exodus 13:21–22). There it is described as a pillar that is a cloud during the day and fire at night. Here, the cloud also looks like fire at night. In this chapter, the cloud visually shows Yahweh’s commands for when and where the Israelites should travel. Be sure that it is clear to your readers that Yahweh controls the cloud.
chapters.10:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter provides the commands Yahweh gave to Moses about silver trumpets to be used for signaling the people. It also describes the order in which the Israelites set out, Moses’ request to Hobab, and the blessings Moses spoke when the sacred chest was picked up at the beginning of each day and set down at the end of each day.

1. Yahweh commands Moses to make silver trumpets and explains their uses (1–10)
2. Israel leaves Sinai and travels in the assigned order (11–28)
3. Moses asks Hobab to accompany Israel and help guide the people (29–32)
4. The ark goes ahead of Israel, and Moses calls on Yahweh when it sets out and rests (33–36)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Trumpets

The trumpets mentioned in this chapter are metal instruments that make a loud sound when people blow into them. This chapter refers to “blowing” the trumpets as well as “blowing an alarm.” These are two different ways of making sounds with the trumpets. It is not clear exactly what sound the “alarm” was. Some scholars think that the sound was very loud. Others think the sound was repeated. Use a general expression in your language, but be sure to distinguish “blowing” and “blowing an alarm.”

### Israel sets out

In 10:11–28, the author describes the order in which the Israelite tribes set out from their camp at Sinai. While the author is explicitly describing the first time they left, he implies that this is also how they normally traveled. The four camps that Yahweh outlined in Numbers 2 set out in the same order in this chapter: east, south, west, north. It is also important to note that the Levites set out in two different groups: first the Gershonites and Merarites, who carried the pieces of the sacred tent, and later the Kohathites, who carried the things that belonged inside the sacred tent.

### “According to their armies”

As in Numbers 2, the phrase “according to their armies” indicates that each tribe and camp was organized and arranged into military units or divisions. The people in each military unit would camp together, and their names were listed together when the census was recorded. The UST expresses this idea with the phrase “by their army divisions.”
chapters.11:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the Israelites complain about the manna that Yahweh provided for them and ask for meat instead. Yahweh gives them meat but also punishes them. Yahweh also appoints 70 men to help Moses lead the Israelites.

1. The people complain, and Yahweh sends fire against the camp (1–3)
2. The people complain about food, and Moses asks Yahweh for help (4–15)
3. Yahweh promises helpers for Moses and meat for the people (16–23)
4. Yahweh gives his Spirit to 70 leaders to help Moses (24–30)
5. Yahweh sends quail and punishes the people (31–35)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The manna

In this chapter, the Israelites complain about the food that Yahweh provided for them, which was called “manna.” See Exodus 16 for more information about how God provided the manna for them. Here, the Israelites want meat instead of manna. God provides them with meat, but he also punishes them for failing to be content with the manna. The author also briefly describes the manner. It is shaped like small seeds, and it has the consistency or color of gum resin.

### The Spirit

In 11:17, 25–26, and 29, the “Spirit” is mentioned. Scholars debate whether the word refers to God’s own Spirit, which he gave to Moses, or whether it refers to Moses’ spirit, which Yahweh had enabled in a special way. Either way, it is clear that Yahweh enabled Moses to lead the Israelites, and now Yahweh also enables the 70 men to lead the Israelites too. It is recommended that you follow the UST and indicate that the Spirit is God’s Spirit. However, also consider how translations that your readers might be familiar with treat the word “Spirit” here.

### Prophesying

In this chapter, Yahweh sends his Spirit on 70 leaders. When they receive the Spirit, they “prophesy.” The author does not indicate exactly what they said or did. In some cases, “prophesying” means not being in control of one’s body and saying strange things. In other cases, “prophesying” means speaking words from God. In this context, it is likely that the leaders “prophesied” by speaking words from God, but they may also have acted strangely as they did so.

### The quails

In this chapter, Yahweh sends birds called “quails” to the Israelites. These birds are good to eat. They are brown and have a wingspan of around 32–35 centimeters. They migrate in large numbers through the Sinai area twice a year.
chapters.12:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses and claim authority like his authority. God punishes Miriam, but then he restores her when Moses intercedes for her.

1. Miriam and Aaron question Moses’ authority (1–3)
2. Yahweh explains Moses’ special role as his servant (4–9)
3. Miriam receives a skin disease and stays outside the camp for seven days (10–16)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Miriam and Aaron

Miriam was Moses’ older sister. Aaron was Moses’ older brother, although Aaron was younger than Miriam. In this story, they claim to have the authority to speak for God as Moses did. However, by the end of the chapter, God has shown that Moses is the one who has this authority.

### Moses’ wife

This chapter refers to a wife of Moses who was a Cushite, which means that she was from the area that is now southern Egypt and northern Sudan. In Exodus 2:21, Moses marries a woman named Zipporah, but it is clear in the context that she is a Midianite (see Exodus 2:16). It is possible that Zipporah could be identified both as a Cushite and as a Midianite. It is more likely that Moses married a second woman, who was a Cushite. However, since the text does not directly identify this woman, it is recommended that you refer to her as generally as 12:1 does.

### Skin disease

God punishes Miriam by making her suffer a skin disease. This specific skin disease disfigures her skin and makes it white. It is not certain exactly what skin disease it is. It is recommended that you use a general term for a skin disease.
chapters.13:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh has Moses send 12 leaders to explore the land of Canaan. They explore it from south to north and then return to the Israelites. They report that the land is good, but most of them discourage the Israelites from going there because the inhabitants are big and strong.

1. Yahweh commands Moses to send leaders to explore the land of Canaan, and Moses gives them instructions (1–20)
2. The leaders explore Canaan and gather fruit (21–25)
3. The leaders report what they have seen, and Caleb urges Israel to take the land (26–33)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Exploring Canaan

In this chapter, Moses sends 12 leaders to explore the land of Canaan. Moses asks them to find out how the area is laid out, how fertile it is, what its people are like, and what their defenses are like. Moses asks for this information because it will help him plan how to take over the area.

### Areas within Canaan

Moses tells the leaders to go from the Negeb in the south to the hill country, which is the central area to the north of the Negeb. When the leaders travel, they go from the wilderness of Zin in the southern part of the region to Lebo Hamath in the northern part of the region. The author also mentions Hebron, which is in the southern part of the hill country, and Wadi Eshcol, whose location is unknown. The mentioned locations indicate that the leaders did explore the entire land of Canaan, from south to north and then back south.

### The Anak and the Nephils

In this chapter, the author mentions that there are “sons of the Anak” living at Hebron. These “Anakites” were tall and powerful men. The author mentions three names: Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai. These could be names of three tribes or, more likely, three men. At the end of the chapter, the Israelite leaders mention “Nephils,” and the author notes that the sons of Anak are a type of Nephil. The Nephils are also mentioned in Genesis 6:4, where they are described as mighty men. Scholars do not agree on exactly what the Nephils and the Anakites were. It is clear that they were tall and powerful people.
chapters.14:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the Israelites refuse to enter Canaan. Yahweh then declares how he will punish them. When the Israelites hear this, they decide to go to Canaan after all. However, Yahweh does not help them, and they are defeated.

1. Israel refuses to enter Canaan despite Joshua and Caleb’s appeal (1–12)
2. Moses asks Yahweh to forgive the people (13–19)
3. Yahweh declares that the rebellious generation will not enter the land (20–38)
4. Israel tries to enter the land without Yahweh’s help and is defeated (39–45)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Murmuring

In this chapter, “murmuring” refers to speaking against someone else. In this context, it means that people say that their leader is doing a bad job leading them. Consider how you would express this idea in your language.

### Forgiveness and punishment

In this chapter, Moses quotes what Yahweh had previously said about himself: he both forgives and punishes. In response to Moses asking Yahweh to forgive the Israelites, that is exactly what Yahweh does. He forgives them, but he also punishes them for their disobedience. More specifically, all the people who refused to go to Canaan will die in the wilderness, but their children will enter and live in Canaan.
chapters.15:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh gives instructions for grain and drink offerings, contributions from first batches of bread, atonement for unintentional sins, punishment for intentional sins, and tassels on clothing. The author also narrates a story about a man who gathered wood on the Sabbath.

1. Yahweh gives instructions for offerings in the land of Canaan (1–21)
2. Yahweh explains how to make offerings for sins committed by mistake (22–29)
3. Yahweh warns against deliberate disobedience (30–31)
4. A man is put to death for breaking the Sabbath law (32–36)
5. Yahweh commands Israel to wear tassels as reminders of his commands (37–41)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Grain and drink offerings

This chapter includes instructions for what the Israelites were supposed to offer along with animal sacrifices. For each male lamb, ram, and bull that they offered, they needed to offer also a specific portion of grain and wine. The portion size was different for each animal. When the Israelites included the grain and drink offerings with each animal, Yahweh was pleased.

### Contributions from first dough

This chapter includes instructions on contributions from the dough that the Israelites made from the first grain that they harvested each year. They were to make one loaf from this dough to give to Yahweh. This contribution would be similar to the contribution that farmers made from the first grain that they harvested. Some scholars think that the contribution of a loaf was specifically intended for Israelites who were not farmers and who did not have grain from a harvest to contribute.

### Deliberate and unintentional sins

This chapter includes information on deliberate and unintentional sins. Deliberate sins are when people know that they are disobeying God and continue to do so anyway. They do not feel any regret or guilt for what they have done. Those people cannot atone for their sins but instead are punished. Unintentional sins are when people disobey God without realizing that they are disobeying. Those people can atone for their sins, and God gives instructions on what sacrifices to offer. Unintentional sins can be committed by many people together or by one person, and the sacrifices are different in these two cases.

### The Sabbath

On the Sabbath, which was the seventh day of the week, the Israelites were not allowed to do any work. See Exodus 20:10 for the basic command. In this chapter, a man does work on the Sabbath (gathering firewood), and the Israelite leaders know that he did something wrong. However, they wait to hear from Yahweh how the man should be punished. Yahweh declares that the Israelites must kill him by throwing stones at him, so that is what they do. This story emphasizes how important keeping the Sabbath is to Yahweh.

### Tassels

This chapter includes instructions on “tassels” that the Israelites were supposed to attach to their clothing. Tassels are groups of threads connected together that hang down from whatever they are attached to. In this case, the Israelites were supposed to attach the tassels to the corners of their garments. The outer garments that the Israelites wore were usually in the shape of a rectangle, so there would be four tassels, one at each corner. Each tassel needed to have one cord or thread of blue in it. These tassels functioned as visual reminders that the Israelites were supposed to think about and obey God’s commands.

### Sojourners

The instructions in this chapter on grain and drink offerings and on atonement for unintentional sins apply to “sojourners” as well as to native Israelites. Sojourners were non-Israelites who lived among the Israelites. They were considered sojourners as long as they lived among the Israelites. The laws that include sojourners indicate that these foreigners could participate in worshiping and honoring Yahweh.
chapters.16:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, three men (Korah, Dathan, and Abiram) lead others in rebelling against Moses and Aaron. They want to be the leaders of the Israelites. However, Yahweh kills them and the people who agreed with them. After that, all the Israelites grumble against Moses and Aaron, and Yahweh begins to kill them too. However, Aaron offers incense for them, and Yahweh spares everyone who is still alive.

1. Korah and other leaders challenge Moses and Aaron (1–19)
2. Yahweh punishes the rebels with the opening of the ground and with fire (20–35)
3. The rebels’ incense burners become a covering for the altar and a warning to Israel (36–40)
4. The people complain, and Aaron makes atonement to stop a plague (41–50)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebel

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, along with many men who agreed with them, rebelled against Moses and Aaron. They argued that all the Israelites were holy, and that Aaron was improperly preventing them from approaching Yahweh. They argued that Moses was a bad leader who had not brought them to a fertile land as he had promised. They think that they should be leaders and priests instead of Moses and Aaron. Moses responds by telling them that they are not really rebelling against Moses and Aaron but against Yahweh, who appointed them. Yahweh then punishes Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and the people who agreed with them.

### The Israelites rebel

After Yahweh punished Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and the people who agreed with them, the rest of the Israelites blame Moses and Aaron for killing them. Yahweh is angry and begins to kill them. Again, when the Israelites rebel against Moses and Aaron, they are rebelling against Yahweh, who appointed them.

### Offering incense

In this chapter, people offer incense in several situations. To offer incense, they put hot coals or embers in a special pan and sprinkled incense on top of them. The incense would burn, creating a smoke that had a pungent smell. Moses had the 250 leaders who agreed with Korah, as well as Korah and Aaron, offer incense in Yahweh’s presence as a test. The person whom Yahweh chose would be the one he wanted to be priest. Later in the chapter, Aaron fulfilled the function of priest by burning incense among the people to make atonement for their sin of speaking against Moses and Aaron. Both times that people burn incense, it proves that Aaron is the real priest.

### The plague

When Yahweh punishes the Israelites for rebelling against Moses and Aaron, he sends a “plague.” The word can refer to many different kinds of disasters. Some translations suggest that the “plague” is a kind of disease. The UST illustrates that option. Other translations use a more general word or phrase that refers to any kind of disaster that kills people.
chapters.17:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses places 13 staffs representing the leaders of the Israelite tribes before Yahweh. Yahweh makes Aaron’s staff blossom and produce nuts, showing that Aaron is the one chosen to be priest. The Israelites then exclaim that they expect to die if they are close to the sacred tent.

1. Yahweh commands each tribal leader to provide a staff (1–7)
2. Aaron’s staff produces buds, blossoms, and almonds (8–11)
3. The people express fear of dying near the tabernacle (12–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The staffs

Yahweh instructs Moses to place 12 staffs in the sacred tent. These staffs represented the leaders of each of the Israelite tribes. That is why each staff had the name of a leader written on it. Yahweh used the staffs to show the Israelites which leader he had chosen to be priest.
chapters.18:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter includes instructions about how the Levites and the priests serve at the sacred tent. It also includes regulations about which sacred things belong to the priests and to the Levites. It concludes with the requirement that the Levites give a tithe to the priests.

1. Yahweh assigns duties to the priests and Levites (1–7)
2. Yahweh gives portions of Israel’s offerings to the priests (8–20)
3. Yahweh gives Israel’s tithes to the Levites for their service (21–24)
4. Yahweh commands the Levites to give a tenth of their tithes to the priests (25–32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Priests and Levites

This chapter indicates that the Levites and the priests are responsible for making sure that no one defiles any of the holy things or places. The priests are responsible especially for the sacred tent and for who acts as a priest. The Levites are responsible for making sure that no one comes near the sacred tent, especially when they are setting it up, taking it down, and moving it. This chapter also makes it clear that the Levites are under the direction of the priests.

### Contributions for the priests

In 18:8–19, Yahweh outlines the contributions from the Israelites that go directly to the priests. These include parts of the grain offering, sin offering, and guilt offering that the priests do not burn. These also include the firstfruits of crops and the firstborn male animals and humans. In the case of humans and clean animals, however, the priests receive money instead of the human or animal. All these contributions are very holy, so Yahweh gives them to the priests specifically.

### Contributions for the Levites

In 18:20–24, Yahweh outlines the contributions from the Israelites that go directly to the Levites. The tithes are made up of one-tenth of all the produce and animals that Israelites have grown or raised. The Israelites give these tithes to Yahweh, and Yahweh gives them to the Levites instead of land.

### Tithes from the Levites

In 18:25–32, Yahweh indicates that the Levites also must give tithes. They tithe directly to the priests. Once the Levites have given their tithes, they can use the rest of what they receive from the Israelites as regular food. It is not considered sacred any longer.
chapters.19:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter explains how people can become clean after contact with a dead person. The ashes of a red cow are mixed with water and used in the cleansing ceremony.

1. Yahweh gives instructions for preparing the ashes of a red cow (1–10)
2. Yahweh explains how to cleanse people and objects made unclean by contact with the dead (11–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Impurity from dead bodies

This chapter explains how dead bodies, including a burial site or even a bone from a body, make people impure. This impurity must be removed quickly. If people come in direct contact with a dead body, they must participate in this specific ritual twice over seven days. Even the person who helps them become pure is unclean until that evening. This chapter indicates how dangerous this kind of impurity is and how the Israelites must remove it.

### Defiling the sacred tent

Because impurity from a dead body is so dangerous, Yahweh requires every Israelite who becomes impure in this way to cleanse themselves immediately. If anyone does not do this, their impurity makes the sacred tent impure, even if they do not visit the sacred tent. Making the sacred tent impure is a very serious crime that Yahweh will punish.

### Priest or clean person

This chapter requires a priest to preside when someone burns the cow to create ashes. However, any clean person can apply the water and ashes to the people who are impure. It does not have to be a priest. In fact, because that clean person becomes unclean when he or she applies the water and ashes, it probably would not have been a priest.
chapters.20:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes the deaths of Miriam and Aaron. It also tells how Moses and Aaron disobey Yahweh when the people need water. Yahweh declares that they will not lead Israel into the Promised Land.

1. Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh (1)
2. Yahweh provides water from a rock, but Moses and Aaron disobey him (2–13)
3. Edom refuses to let Israel travel through its land (14–21)
4. Aaron dies, and Eleazar takes his place as high priest (22–29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### What Moses and Aaron did wrong

In 20:12, Yahweh condemns Moses and Aaron for doing something wrong when they provided water for the people. However, Yahweh does not specify exactly which action was wrong, and scholars debate what it was. Yahweh told Moses to speak to the rock, but Moses also struck it twice with a staff. That may have been what he did wrong. Moses also spoke to the people as if he and Aaron were the ones providing the water. This may have implied that it was them instead of Yahweh. That may have been what he did wrong. Since the text does not make it explicit, it is recommended that you do not state exactly which action was wrong in your translation.

### Transferring clothing

In 20:26–28, Moses must take Aaron’s clothing off and put it on his son Eleazar. This clothing was specifically the clothing that Aaron wore when he did his work as high priest. Moses only removed Aaron’s outer garments. He did not make Aaron completely naked. When Moses transferred the high priest clothing from Aaron to Eleazar, it symbolized that Eleazar was now high priest.
chapters.21:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes Israel’s journey toward Moab and victories over enemy kings. When the people complain, Yahweh sends poisonous snakes. He then provides a way for those who are bitten to live.

1. Yahweh helps Israel defeat the king of Arad at the Battle of Hormah (1–3)
2. Yahweh sends poisonous snakes and tells Moses to make a bronze snake (4–9)
3. Israel continues the journey toward Moab (10–20)
4. Israel defeats Sihon and takes his land (21–32)
5. Israel defeats Og and takes his land (33–35)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The bronze serpent

In 21:4–9, the author narrates how the Israelites complained, and God punished them by sending venomous snakes that bit them. When the Israelites ask for forgiveness and help, Yahweh has Moses create a model of a serpent made from bronze. When any Israelite had been bitten by a snake, he or she could look at the model and would recover. The author does not explain how this works, so your translation also should not state that explicitly.

### Citations of poetry

In this chapter, the author cites parts of three different pieces of poetry. Each citation supports a claim that the author has made. In 21:14–15, the citation proves that the Arnon River is the border for Moab. In 21:17–18, the citation identifies which story about a well the author is speaking about. In 21:27–30, the citation proves that Sihon captured Heshbon and its territory from the Moabites. It may also prove that the Israelites defeated Sihon. Consider how you might naturally introduce and format citations of poetry that support claims the author is making.
chapters.22:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter introduces Balak, the king of Moab, and Balaam. Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel. On Balaam’s journey, Yahweh uses a donkey and an angel to warn him to speak only what Yahweh tells him.

1. Israel camps in Moab, and Balak sends for Balaam (1–20)
2. Balaam’s donkey sees Yahweh’s angel, and the angel warns Balaam (21–35)
3. Balak welcomes Balaam and takes him to see part of Israel’s camp (36–41)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cursing

In Balak and Balaam’s culture, people believed that certain people made more effective curses than others. Balaam was a person who could make an effective curse. Balak wants Balaam to say, with words, bad things that would happen to the Israelites. Then, these bad things would actually happen. People in this culture believed that this kind of curse would work because one of the gods would make the bad things happen. Consider how you might refer to spoken words that cause bad things to happen to people.

### Balaam’s profession

Numbers 22:7 indicates that Balak’s messengers brought “divinations” with them to Balaam. This indicates that Balaam’s profession was “diviner,” and Joshua 13:22 confirms this by calling Balaam a “diviner.” Divination included several different ways of receiving messages from gods. That included prophecy (speaking directly for a god or gods), receiving and interpreting dreams, and examining events (like the flight of birds) or animal entrails. Balaam encounters God in dreams, speaks for God, and participates in offering sacrifices. All these actions fit with his profession of diviner. Consider how you might refer to this kind of person in your translation.

### Why was God angry with Balaam?

God permits Balaam to go with the messengers from Balak. However, once Balaam leaves, God is angry with him for going (22:22). The author does not indicate why God is angry. Some have speculated that Balaam’s intentions are wrong (he only wants money, or he intends to say something contrary to what God wants). Others guess that Balaam is unable to understand what God wants, and so God has to open his eyes. It is recommended that you leave the tension in your translation without explaining it. This best represents what the author of the narrator chose to include.
chapters.23:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Balaam pronounces two separate oracles that bless Israel. The first oracle focuses on how God has blessed Israel when Balak wants Balaam to curse Israel. The second oracle focuses on how God has acted for the Israelites and how strong the Israelites are.

1. Balaam gives his first message and blesses Israel (1–12)
2. Balaam gives his second message and explains that God’s blessing cannot be reversed (13–26)
3. Balak takes Balaam to another place to try again (27–30)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Oracles

The word translated “oracle” in verses 7 and 18 is often translated “proverb” or “parable” in other places. Balaam’s speeches are too long to be considered proverbs. In this case, the word “oracle” may indicate that Balaam is speaking in paired lines (see the paragraph on “Parallelism” below) or perhaps that he has put together multiple statements that are like proverbs. Either way, it is clear that Balaam is speaking as a prophet when he delivers these oracles. Consider what word you might use to refer to poetic, prophetic speech.

### Blessing and cursing

See the chapter introduction to Numbers 22 for more information on cursing. People in this culture believed that specific words, spoken by specific people, would have either good or bad effects. The words that led to good effects were blessings, and the words that led to bad effects were curses. In this chapter, Balak asks Balaam to curse the Israelites, but Balaam actually blesses them, as Yahweh commands him to do.

### Different locations

After each of Balaam’s oracles in this chapter, Balak requests that they move to a different location and try again. The author does not state why Balak thinks that a change in location will help Balaam curse the Israelites instead of bless them. He may have thought that a different perspective would change Balaam’s mind. He may have thought that God only had power to control Balaam in certain places. Or he may have thought something else. In your translation, it should be clear that Balaam thinks that a change in location will be helpful, but it is recommended that you do not make explicit why Balak thinks the change in location will help.
chapters.24:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Balaam pronounces two more oracles that bless Israel. The first oracle focuses on how prosperous and powerful Israel will be. The second oracle focuses on a future leader of the Israelites. Finally, Balaam gives three short oracles about other nearby nations.

1. Balaam gives his third oracle, describing Israel’s future prosperity and strength (1–14)
2. Balaam gives his fourth oracle, announcing a future ruler who will defeat Israel’s enemies (15–19)
3. Balaam gives three short oracles about other nations and then leaves (20–25)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Oracles

The word translated “oracle” in verses 3, 15, 20, 21, and 23 is often translated “proverb” or “parable” in other places. Balaam’s speeches are usually too long to be considered proverbs. In this case, the word “oracle” may indicate that Balaam is speaking in paired lines (see the paragraph on “Parallelism” below) or perhaps that he has put together multiple statements that are like proverbs. Either way, it is clear that Balaam is speaking as a prophet when he delivers these oracles. Consider what word you might use to refer to poetic, prophetic speech.

### Blessing and cursing

See the chapter introduction to Numbers 21 for more information on cursing. People in this culture believed that specific words, spoken by specific people, would have either good or bad effects. The words that led to good effects were blessings, and the words that led to bad effects were curses. In this chapter, Balak wants Balaam to curse the Israelites, but Balaam actually blesses them, as Yahweh commands him to do.

### A prophecy about the Messiah?

Balaam’s final oracle (24:15–19) seems to refer to a specific person who will be a special ruler of Israel. Scholars debate whether this specific person is David, a future Messiah, or both. The oracle itself is not totally clear about who this person will be and what this person will do. It is recommended that your translation does not make explicit whether some earlier ruler, the Messiah, or both are the subject of the oracle.
chapters.25:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the Israelites worship Baal of Peor with the Moabites, and God punishes them. Then Phinehas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman who are involved in the worship, and this atones for the Israelites. God then blesses Phinehas. He also tells the Israelites to attack the Midianites.

1. Israel worships Baal of Peor, and Yahweh commands punishment (1–5)
2. Phinehas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, and the plague stops (6–9)
3. Yahweh promises Phinehas and his descendants a lasting priesthood (10–13)
4. The man and woman are identified, and Yahweh commands Israel to attack Midian (14–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### What were the Israelites doing wrong?

Scholars debate what the Israelites were doing with the Midianite and Moabite women in this chapter. Some think that the Israelites were participating in cultic sexual acts with the women as part of their worship of Baal. Others think that the Israelites were marrying the women and then participating with their wives in the worship of Baal. Either way, it is clear that Israelite men were interacting with the Moabite and Midianite women, and these interactions led to the Israelites worshiping Baal. It is recommended that your translation does not indicate explicitly whether cultic sexual activity or marriage was happening.

### Midianites and Moabites

In 25:1, the author indicates that the Moabites are the ones who convinced the Israelites to worship Baal. However, the woman whom Phinehas kills for doing this is a Midianite (see 25:6). Further, when Yahweh tells the Israelites to attack the people who convinced them to worship Baal, he identifies those people as the Midianites. Most likely, this area was populated by both Midianites and Moabites, and both groups of people were probably involved. So, you should leave references to both Moabites and Midianites in this chapter.
chapters.26:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses and Eleazar take a census of the Israelite men who are at least 20 years old and who can be soldiers. They count the Levites separately. This census shows that none of the men counted in the first census are still alive except for Moses, Caleb, and Joshua.

1. Moses and Eleazar count Israel’s fighting men by tribe (1–51)
2. Yahweh explains how the land is to be divided (52–56)
3. The Levites are counted separately (57–62)
4. The count confirms that the earlier generation has died, except for Caleb and Joshua (63–65)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Census

In this census, Moses and Eleazar list all the Israelite men who are able to fight or, in the case of the Levites, to serve at the sacred tent. They list the men by their clans, which are subgroups within tribes. While the author uses different words in this chapter, the general format is similar to chapter 1. See how you translated the census record there.

### Subclans

For every tribe, the author lists major clans that make up that tribe. In some cases, the author also lists smaller groups within those clans. These smaller groups are sometimes called subclans. Consider what terminology you might use for major groups within a tribe and the smaller groups that make up those major groups.

### Dividing the land

In 26:53–56, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide the land up among the tribes. He indicates that larger groups should receive more land than smaller groups. He also indicates that the Israelites should cast lots to see who gets what land. Scholars debate how these two strategies work together. It seems most probable that the Israelites cast lots to see where their land would be, and then they decided on the size of the area based on the size of the tribal group. The author does not directly state whether the lots were cast for each tribe, for each clan, or for each individual. Because the census earlier in the chapter focuses on individual clans, the UST indicates that these instructions are about clans.

### Lots

In 26:53–56, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide up the land among the Israelites. These instructions include using lots. Using lots was a way to randomize decisions. Lots could be cast, which would mean rolling or throwing marked stones or pieces of wood to see which side would land upright. Lots could be drawn, which would mean picking marked items without looking at the marks. In this culture, people believed that the decisions, although random from a human perspective, were directed by God. Consider how you might refer to this way of making decisions, which removes human choice but leaves open divine choice.

### The Levites

In 26:57–62. Moses and Eleazar count the Levites. The author states why the Levites are counted separately. They do not receive land, so they are not counted among the rest of the Israelites in this census. Additionally, every male who is at least one month old is counted, unlike the rest of the Israelites, who are counted if they are at least 20 years old. The placement of the Levites after the list of the rest of the Israelites shows that the Levites are set apart for God.
chapters.27:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter explains how a man’s daughters can inherit his property if he has no sons. It also describes how Yahweh chooses Joshua to lead Israel after Moses.

1. Zelophehad’s daughters ask to inherit their father’s property, and Yahweh gives a law about inheritance (1–11)
2. Yahweh tells Moses that he will see the Promised Land but will not enter it (12–14)
3. Moses asks for a new leader, and Yahweh chooses Joshua (15–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Children and inheritance

In this culture, when a father died, his sons usually inherited his land and property. This practice maintained land and property within one group that was descended from a single ancestor. In this chapter, the daughters of a man who had no sons make a request. They want to inherit their father’s land and property. That way, a portion of their tribe’s land will continue to belong to the descendants of their father, just like it will for their father’s brothers. Yahweh agrees that this is the right thing to do. Daughters should inherit their father’s land and property if there are no sons. Only if there are also no daughters should the land and property be inherited by other relatives, like brothers or uncles.

### Commissioning Joshua

When Moses learns that he will soon die, he asks Yahweh to appoint a leader who will replace him. Yahweh tells Moses to commission Joshua. Joshua will only share some of Moses’ glory, and he will have to communicate with God through the high priest instead of directly. However, he will be the next leader of the Israelites. Moses signifies this by laying his hands on Joshua.
chapters.28:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh gives instructions concerning the animals, grain, and wine that the Israelites needed to offer to him on certain days. That includes offerings for every day, for Sabbath days, for the first days of months, for the Festival of Unleavened Bread, and for the day of firstfruits during the Festival of Weeks.

1. Yahweh gives instructions for daily offerings (1–8)
2. Yahweh gives instructions for Sabbath offerings (9–10)
3. Yahweh gives instructions for monthly offerings (11–15)
4. Yahweh gives instructions for Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread (16–25)
5. Yahweh gives instructions for the Festival of Weeks (26–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Grain and drink offerings

This chapter includes instructions for what the Israelites were supposed to offer along with animal sacrifices. For each male lamb, ram, and bull that they offered, they needed to offer also a specific portion of grain and wine. The portion size was different for each animal. When the Israelites included the grain and drink offerings with each animal, Yahweh was pleased.
chapters.29:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh continues to give instructions concerning the animals, grain, and wine that the Israelites needed to offer to him on certain days. That includes the first day of the seventh month (sometimes called the Festival of Trumpets), the tenth day of the seventh month (the Day of Atonement), the seven-day festival that began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (the Festival of Huts), and the day immediately after the Festival of Huts.

1. Yahweh gives instructions for the Festival of Trumpets (1–6)
2. Yahweh gives instructions for the Day of Atonement (7–11)
3. Yahweh gives instructions for the Festival of Huts and the final assembly (12–38)
4. Moses passes Yahweh’s instructions on to Israel (39–40)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Grain and drink offerings

This chapter includes instructions for what the Israelites were supposed to offer along with animal sacrifices. For each male lamb, ram, and bull that they offered, they needed to offer also a specific portion of grain and wine. The portion size was different for each animal. When the Israelites included the grain and drink offerings with each animal, Yahweh was pleased.
chapters.30:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses recounts instructions concerning vows and agreements made by women. The instructions deal with four situations: an unmarried woman living with her parents, a woman who has recently gotten married, a divorced woman or widow, and a woman who is married. In each case, if the woman is part of a man’s household, the man is responsible for confirming or nullifying the woman’s vow or agreement.

1. Moses explains that vows made to Yahweh must be kept (1–2)
2. A father may confirm or cancel the vow of a young woman living in his house (3–5)
3. A husband may confirm or cancel a vow his wife made before their marriage (6–8)
4. Widows and divorced women must keep their vows (9)
5. Moses explains the rules for vows made by married women (10–16)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Household structure and authority

In this culture, the person who had authority over the whole household was the oldest male. So, a daughter living at home with her parents or a married woman living with her husband was under the authority of the man, whether her father or her husband. However, for a widow or divorced woman, there was no man with authority over her. Given this way of structuring households, this chapter indicates that the person in charge of the household (usually the husband or father) was responsible for confirming or nullifying any promises or agreements made by the women in the household.

### Vows

Vows were promises that a person made to God. Often, the person would ask God to do something and then promise to do something or give something to God if God did what the person asked. Consider how you might refer to this kind of solemn promise made to God.

### Oaths

Oaths were statements that confirmed promises and commitments. Oaths could call God as witness, or they could specify the consequences if the promise or commitment was broken. Consider how you might refer to this kind of solemn confirming statement.

### Bonds

The word translated as “bond” in this chapter occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Scholars debate exactly what it means. It could refer to a promise not to do something, while “vow” refers to a promise to do something. More likely, it refers to a binding agreement, sometimes written, with a person or people. The UST follows that interpretation. Consider how you might refer to a binding agreement between people.
chapters.31:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes Israel’s war against Midian. After the battle, Moses gives instructions about the captives and about cleansing the soldiers and captured goods. The goods are divided, and portions are given to Yahweh.

1. Yahweh commands Israel to attack Midian, and Israel wins the battle (1–12)
2. Moses gives instructions about the captives and purification after battle (13–24)
3. The captives, animals, and goods are divided, with portions given to Yahweh (25–47)
4. The army’s officers bring gold as an offering to Yahweh (48–54)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### War for Yahweh

When the Israelites fought wars that Yahweh commanded them to fight, they sometimes killed all the men of the people they were fighting. That is what they do when they defeat the Midianites in this chapter. While God does not give explicit instructions, Moses also requires the Israelites to kill the boys and the women who have had sex. These actions are very violent, and scholars interpret the meaning in different ways. It is recommended that translations simply represent the violence.

### Purity and impurity

This chapter refers back to concepts that were important in Numbers 19. Those concepts include impurity because of dead bodies and the special water that the Israelites could use to cleanse this impurity. In this chapter, the soldiers, captives, and plunder are impure. The people must be cleansed by washing with the special water as they wait outside the camp for seven days. The plunder must be cleansed by the special water and, in some cases, by fire. Once everything is cleansed, the people and plunder may enter the Israelite camp.

### The levy for Yahweh and the Levites

This chapter refers to a “levy” from the plunder that the Israelites needed to pay to Yahweh and to the Levites. Moses first divided the plunder in half. One half was for the soldiers who had fought in the battle. From this half, they had to give one out of every 500 people and animals to Yahweh as the “levy.” Yahweh then granted this levy to Eleazar and the rest of the priests. From the other half that belonged to the rest of the Israelites, they had to give one out of every 50 people and animals to the Levites. Some translations refer to this “levy” as a tax or a tribute. Consider how you might refer to the levy in your language.
chapters.32:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses, Joshua, Eleazar, and the Israelite leaders make an agreement with the leaders of the tribes of Gad and Reuben. This agreement specifies that the soldiers from Gad and Reuben must help the rest of the Israelites conquer the land west of the Jordan River. However, once that is done, the people of Gad and Reuben receive land on the east side of the Jordan River. The chapter also briefly recounts some people from Manasseh who also conquered and received land on the east side of the Jordan River.

1. Reuben and Gad ask to settle east of the Jordan (1–5)
2. Moses warns them against discouraging the other Israelites from entering Canaan (6–15)
3. Reuben and Gad promise to help the other tribes take the land (16–27)
4. Moses confirms the agreement and gives land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh (28–42)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Land on the east side and west side of the Jordan River

The land of Canaan itself was on the west side of the Jordan River. However, the Israelites conquered some land on the east side of the Jordan River. People from Gad, Reuben, and part of the tribe of Manasseh wanted to receive this land on the east side of the Jordan. Moses initially rejects their desire, but eventually he allows them to receive this land as long as they help the rest of the Israelites conquer the land of Canaan on the west side of the Jordan River.
chapters.33:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the narrator records places where the Israelites camped on the way from Egypt to the plains of Moab. At the end of the chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how the Israelites should conquer and divide the land.

1. Moses records the stages of Israel’s journey (1–2)
2. Israel’s journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab is listed (3–49)
3. Yahweh commands Israel to drive out Canaan’s inhabitants, destroy their places of worship, and divide the land (50–56)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Dividing the land

In 33:54, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide the land up among the tribes. He indicates that larger groups should receive more land than smaller groups. He also indicates that the Israelites should cast lots to see who gets what land. Scholars debate how these two strategies work together. It seems most probable that the Israelites cast lots to see where their land would be, and then they decided on the size of the area based on the size of the tribal group. See how you translated the similar instructions in 26:53–56.

### Lots

In 33:54, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide up the land among the Israelites. These instructions include using lots. Using lots was a way to randomize decisions. Lots could be cast, which would mean rolling or throwing marked stones or pieces of wood to see which side would land upright. Lots could be drawn, which would mean picking marked items without looking at the marks. In this culture, people believed that the decisions, although random from a human perspective, were directed by God. Consider how you might refer to this way of making decisions, which removes human choice but leaves open divine choice. See how you translated the instructions concerning lots in 26:53–56.
chapters.34:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes the borders of the land Israel will receive in Canaan. Yahweh also names the leaders who will divide the land among the tribes.

1. Yahweh describes Canaan’s southern, western, northern, and eastern borders (1–12)
2. Moses explains which tribes will receive land west of the Jordan (13–15)
3. Yahweh names the leaders who will divide the land (16–29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The borders of Canaan

In the first part of this chapter, Yahweh outlines the borders of Canaan. He describes a shape that is almost a rectangle. He starts at the southeast corner, which is the bottom of the Sea of Salt. The south side is a curved line from there to the Mediterranean Sea. The west side simply follows the Mediterranean Sea. The north side begins in the west at the Mediterranean Sea and goes east, somewhere above the Sea of Chinnereth. The east side begins somewhere above the Sea of Chinnereth and goes south to the southern part of the Sea of Salt. While the Israelites did not succeed in conquering all this territory, this is the area that Yahweh instructed them to conquer.

### Inheriting the land

In the second half of this chapter, Yahweh speaks of leaders “inheriting the land.” This phrase refers to the process of dividing the land up into sections. The leaders would then assign each section to a tribal group or family. They would do this using lots (see the chapter introduction to Numbers 33 for more information on lots). Yahweh ensures that at least one leader from each tribe was involved in this process.
chapters.35:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter gives instructions for towns and pastureland for the Levites. Six towns will be places of refuge for people who kill someone by accident. The chapter explains how to distinguish murder (intentional killing) from manslaughter (unintentional killing) and how each case must be handled.

1. Yahweh commands Israel to give towns and pastureland to the Levites (1–8)
2. Yahweh commands Israel to set apart six cities of refuge (9–15)
3. Yahweh gives laws about murder, manslaughter, and protection in cities of refuge (16–29)
4. Yahweh requires witnesses for a murder conviction and forbids payments that would cancel the required punishment (30–34)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cities of refuge

Six of the cities that the Israelites were supposed to give to the Levites functioned as cities of refuge. When a person killed someone, he or she normally deserved to be killed by the dead person’s close relative. However, if the person killed someone by accident, the person could flee to one of the six cities. If he or she stayed in that city, the dead person’s close relative was not allowed to kill him or her. In this way, the city provided refuge, or safety, for someone who unintentionally killed someone else. Eventually, that person would stand trial to confirm whether they killed someone unintentionally or intentionally.

### One redeeming the blood

This chapter describes a close relative of a person who was killed as “one redeeming the blood.” This phrase fits with what Yahweh says in 35:33–34. When a person kills someone (sheds their blood), redemption or atonement needs to be accomplished. The close relative could accomplish this redemption by killing the murderer. In this way, they “redeemed the blood” of their relative and made things right before God.

### Intentional and unintentional killing

This chapter distinguishes carefully between intentional killing (murder) and unintentional killing (manslaughter). The criteria for deciding between murder and manslaughter include the weapon used, the way the person died, the relationship between the people, and whether the action was intentional or accidental. Consider what words you might use to distinguish between murder (intentional killing) and manslaughter (unintentional killing).

### The death of the high priest

Yahweh indicates that a person who killed someone unintentionally would have to stay in a city of refuge until the high priest died. What the high priest’s death accomplishes is not directly stated. Most likely, the high priest’s death atoned for all the unintentional killings during his time as high priest. This is like the sacrifices offered on the Day of the Atonement, which atoned for many sins committed throughout the year. However, since Yahweh does not make the function of the high priest’s death explicit, it is recommended that you also do not make it explicit in your translation.

### Polluting the land

In 35:33–34, Yahweh explains that whenever someone is killed, it pollutes or defiles the land where the Israelites live. This is not good, since Yahweh was present with the Israelites in the land. Because Yahweh was present, both the Israelites and their land needed to be pure. So, it was very important for the Israelites to deal with murder and manslaughter properly. Only executing a murderer and keeping a manslayer in a city of refuge would keep the land pure. These verses provide the motivation for following the commands earlier in the chapter.
chapters.36:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses gives Yahweh’s instructions concerning keeping ancestral land within a tribe when daughters inherit that land. He gives specific instructions for Zelophehad’s daughters, which continue from 27:1–11, and then more general instructions. Daughters that inherit land must marry someone from the same tribe to keep ancestral land within that tribe. The chapter ends with a brief conclusion to this section of Numbers.

1. Manasseh’s clan leaders raise a concern about land passing to another tribe through marriage (1–4)
2. Yahweh commands women who inherit land to marry within their father’s tribe (5–9)
3. Zelophehad’s daughters obey and marry within their tribe (10–12)
4. Closing summary of the commands given on the plains of Moab (13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Property, marriage, and inheritance

In this culture, when a woman married a man, the man would be in charge of any property or possessions that the woman had. If the woman had inherited land from her father, that land would now belong to her husband. If the husband was from a different tribe than the wife, the land would permanently belong to a different tribe than the tribe of the wife’s father. This situation is what the leaders of Manasseh wish to avoid. Yahweh tells Moses to agree with them and require women who have inherited land to marry within their tribe. That way, the property would continue to belong to their father’s tribe.
